\synth{I relapsed after that experience. For six months I was back to restricting and purging. The images of my body swelling came back every time I looked in a mirror. My weight dropped to a dangerous level and I had to go back into treatment. I felt betrayed by the idea that psychedelics could heal everything.} & \synth{15.71} & \synth{15.71} \\
\synth{Health anxiety and anger at myself. For months I was afraid of any medication. I also felt guilty about lying to the retreat. My depression got worse for a while because I was too scared to restart the SSRI.} & \synth{14.17} & \synth{14.17} \\
\synth{Nervous around dogs for a while, not a big deal.} & \synth{12.83} & \textbf{\synth{\ensuremath{-}12.83}} \\
\synth{Sad about nature for a few days, then fine. Made me appreciate life more.} & \synth{12.31} & \textbf{\synth{\ensuremath{-}12.31}} \\
\synth{The sound from the courtyard is the core of it. I hear it in my head several times a week, sometimes several times a day, even now, two and a half years later. It comes when something heavy falls, when someone drops a bag, sometimes for no reason at all. When it comes I see M on the cobblestones and feel my hand on his jacket. I developed an intense fear of heights and of balconies. I can't stand near a window on an upper floor. In the hospital, where I now work as a junior doctor, I avoid the windows in the higher wards. When I see someone sitting on a wall or a railing I have to look away and my heart races. The doubt about whether I pushed him is the worst part. Rationally, I know I didn't. M doesn't blame me. The police closed the case. But the feeling that my hand might have pushed rather than grabbed comes back again and again. It's like a splinter. The guilt about not helping properly is also huge. I was supposed to be the one who knew first aid. During my emergency medicine rotation, the first time I had to assist with a trauma patient who had fallen, I froze and had to leave the room. My supervisor was kind but I was humiliated. I had nightmares nearly every night in the first year. Moons, balconies, falling. Sometimes I'm the one falling. I'd wake up with my hand reaching out. I became depressed. I thought about quitting medical school. I felt like a fraud, how could I be a doctor if I froze when it mattered? I withdrew from most of the friends who were at the party, because being with them brought it back. I drank a lot in the first months. I also had periods of feeling unreal, like I was watching my life from the outside, mostly in the weeks after. That faded.} & \synth{12.13} & \synth{12.13} \\
\synth{Since that night I've had chronic depersonalisation and derealisation. It's been two and a half years. I often feel like I'm not fully in my body, like part of me is still floating somewhere. Looking in the mirror is strange. The world often looks flat and dreamlike. I also feel emotionally numb, like the feelings are behind glass. My breakup, which I was trying to escape from, still hurt, but in a weird, muted way. I've been depressed most of the time since. Not because of the breakup anymore, but because I feel I've lost my connection to myself. I've had times where I didn't see the point of going on like this. I don't enjoy things the way I used to. I play guitar and it feels mechanical now. I have a lot of anxiety about the DP, I check myself all the time, and sometimes I have panic attacks where I'm afraid I'll 'leave' my body completely again. I can't sleep on my back because that's how I was lying that night.} & \synth{11.57} & \synth{11.57} \\
\synth{Some anxiety about drugs and my heart for a while. Learned to test everything.} & \synth{11.56} & \textbf{\synth{\ensuremath{-}13.68}} \\
\synth{The weeks after that night were the start of the worst depression I've had. I'm not sure if it was the drugs, or the feeling of being abandoned, or both. I couldn't get out of bed, I didn't want to see anyone, I cried a lot for no clear reason. I couldn't feel anything good, food had no taste, music sounded like noise. I had a strong feeling that nobody actually cares about me and that my friends just tolerated me. I stopped answering their messages, which of course made it worse. Around two months later I started having suicidal thoughts every day. I didn't act on them but I thought about it a lot and looked things up. I had a lot of anxiety too, mostly in social situations, I was convinced that people were laughing at me behind my back. It took over a year for the depression to lift. I lost my job during that time because I couldn't work. I also lost most of my friends from that group. I've made new friends since, but I still find it hard to trust people.} & \synth{11.29} & \synth{11.29} \\
\synth{Nach der Zeremonie kamen immer mehr Erinnerungen an den Missbrauch hoch, die ich jahrelang verdraengt hatte. Ich hatte Flashbacks im Alltag, z.B. beim Duschen oder wenn mich jemand von hinten beruehrt hat. Ich hatte fast jede Nacht Albtraeume und bin schweissgebadet aufgewacht. Meine Depression wurde viel schlimmer statt besser, ich konnte monatelang nicht arbeiten. Ich hatte auch Suizidgedanken. Gleichzeitig habe ich das Gefuehl, dass diese Erinnerungen irgendwann sowieso gekommen waeren, und dass ich jetzt endlich weiss, was mit mir los ist. Aber der Zeitpunkt und die Art, wie es passiert ist, waren furchtbar.} & \synth{10.28} & \synth{10.28} \\
\synth{The months after that night were the worst of my life, and I'm only now, three years later, starting to feel like myself. Nightmares. Almost every night for the first six months. Always water, black water, closing over my head, J's face, his empty eyes, his screaming. I'd wake up gasping, sometimes I'd wake up already out of bed, standing in the room. My partner started sleeping in the guest room because I was thrashing so much. Flashbacks. The smell of lake water, the sound of someone shouting, blue lights, a cold shower. Any of these could send me straight back. Once I was at a public swimming pool with my niece and someone jumped in next to me and I had a full flashback. I was back in the lake. I had to leave immediately and sit in the car shaking for an hour, and my sister had to take my niece home. Avoidance. I couldn't go near lakes, rivers or the sea. I stopped swimming. I stopped going hiking, which had been my favourite thing. I couldn't watch films with water scenes or with people being restrained. I avoided J for a long time, and when I finally saw him, he didn't remember most of what happened and didn't seem very affected, and that made me feel crazy, like I was the only one carrying it. Guilt. Massive guilt. We took the LSD without a sober sitter. I should have noticed that J was off earlier. I held him down. I kept going over it in my head, what I should have done differently. I felt responsible for his psychosis, even though his psychiatrist later told him that he probably had a predisposition. Depression. I lost interest in things. I stopped seeing the other two friends from that weekend because seeing them brought it all back. I stopped going out. My work suffered and I eventually took two months of sick leave. Hypervigilance. I became very jumpy. I'd startle at doors slamming. I couldn't relax in groups because I was always watching people's eyes, looking for that empty look that J had. Derealisation. For the first few months, especially, the world felt unreal, like a stage set. Sometimes I wasn't sure if I had actually survived the lake. That sounds crazy but it was a real feeling, that maybe I had drowned and this was some kind of afterlife. Drinking. I started drinking more to fall asleep. Not to a dangerous level, but more than I should have. The first anniversary was particularly bad. I had a week of panic attacks around that time.} & \synth{10.10} & \synth{10.10} \\
\synth{The months after the circle were a different kind of darkness from the grief I'd had before. I had pneumonia from the exposure, which took weeks to recover from. But the worst was in my mind. I had a recurring image of my son at the edge of the slope, his broken face, beckoning. It came at night mostly, but also in the daytime. Sometimes I'd be at the kitchen sink and suddenly feel the cold stones under my body. I felt drawn towards death in a way I hadn't before. Not actively suicidal, but a pull, like the feeling on the mountain that it would be right to go with him. That frightened me and my husband very much. My grief, which had been heavy but at least clear, became tangled with confusion. Had I really been with my son? Had he wanted me to die? Was it the drug? I couldn't tell anymore what was real. I felt deep shame about what I had done, and also anger at the facilitators, who I felt had nearly let me die and then called it a gift. I stopped going to yoga because I couldn't face the woman who had recommended it. I became more depressed than I had ever been. I barely left the house for six months.} & \synth{10.06} & \synth{10.06} \\
